did_you_know.text: The title identifies the psalm as a “maskil of David” and indicates that it is intended to be performed with musical accompaniment, making it a prayerful psalm with both musical and instructional qualities.
The poet describes his fear in vivid physical terms: his heart is “in anguish,” and the terrors of death fall upon him, expressing the intensity of his emotional distress.
The image of the dove expresses the poet’s desire for escape: he wishes for wings so that he could fly away from danger rather than confront it directly.
The poet asks the Lord to confuse the enemies’ speech because the city is portrayed as a place of violence, conflict, and power struggles.
The city is described as a place where evil operates without pause: “day and night” it surrounds the city, and within it are wickedness, trouble, oppression, and deceit.
The deepest pain comes not from an external enemy but from someone who was close to the poet; if it had been an enemy, the poet could have endured the insult and hidden from him.
The betrayer is described as “my equal and my close friend”—someone familiar and near to the poet—so his betrayal carries special emotional weight in the psalm.
After describing fear and betrayal, the poet declares a constant pattern of turning to God: he calls upon Him in faith that the Lord will save him.
The prayer is offered at three times of day—morning, noon, and evening—emphasizing the poet’s persistence in prayer and supplication.
The psalm contrasts smooth, pleasant speech with violent intent: the enemy’s words are smooth as oil, but his heart is set on war, and his words become like swords.
